noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand how the kidney carries out its roles of excretion and osmoregulation

primer.text: The kidneys hold two job descriptions at once: they scrub urea and surplus ions from the blood, and they hold the body's water content steady. You have met the water story in the ADH note; here you see why it matters — what osmosis would do to cells if the balance slipped.

lessons.title: The Two Roles of the Kidney
lessons.opening: Tucked against the back of the abdominal wall, each kidney filters blood continuously. One role is excretion: stripping out urea and any ion present in excess. The other is osmoregulation: adjusting how much water leaves, so blood pressure and cell conditions stay where they should be. Waste removal and water control are two faces of the same filtering work — as blood passes through, urea and excess ions are picked out for disposal while the water content is tuned by how much the ducts reclaim.
keyPoints: The kidneys sit at the back of the abdomen and filter the blood.
Role one is excretion: urea and surplus ions leave in urine.
Role two is osmoregulation: the water content of the blood is held steady.
Steady water content protects blood pressure as well as the cells.
Both roles run together in every pass of blood through the kidneys.

low.restatement: The kidney cleans the blood of waste and also decides how much water to keep.
low.analogy: One machine, two outputs: a waste pipe and a water tap, both running from the same filter.
low.examPointer: Learn the two roles as a pair — questions frequently name one and ask for the other.

medium.restatement: Excretion removes waste; osmoregulation holds water steady — one organ, both jobs.
medium.analogy: A water-treatment plant that also meters the supply: it cleans and it rations.
medium.examPointer: If a question names only one role, volunteer the second for the remaining marks.

check.stem: Which two roles do the kidneys perform?

options.text: Excretion of waste and regulation of blood water content
options.explanation: These are the two functions named for the kidneys.
Those belong to the gut, not the kidneys.
Gas exchange is the lungs'; temperature control is largely skin and brain.
The heart pumps; plasma is made elsewhere and the kidneys only filter it.

check.stem: Why is holding blood water steady important for blood pressure?

options.text: Water volume determines how much the blood presses on vessel walls
options.explanation: More water means more volume and higher pressure; less means the reverse.

options.text: Water content changes the number of red cells directly
options.explanation: Cell counts are not what water adjusts here.

options.text: Pressure rises only when kidneys fail entirely
options.explanation: Even normal fluctuation shifts pressure; failure is not required.

options.text: Blood pressure is fixed by the heart alone
options.explanation: The heart drives flow, but volume — set by the kidneys — sets the pressure too.

check.stem: Where in the body are the kidneys located?

options.text: At the back of the abdomen
options.explanation: That is the described position of the kidneys.

options.text: Behind the ribs in the chest
options.explanation: That is thorax territory, home of the lungs and heart.
The bladder sits low; the kidneys sit higher, behind the abdomen.

options.text: Either side of the spine at neck level
options.explanation: No organ filters blood at neck level.

check.stem: Which waste is the headline product of the kidney's excretory role?

options.explanation: Urea is the nitrogen waste the kidneys are known for removing.
That is the lungs' cargo.
Not part of this specification's kidney story.
Bile belongs to the liver's digestive outputs.

check.stem: What joins the two kidney roles into one process?

options.text: Both come from the same filtration of blood through nephrons
options.explanation: One filtering machine delivers both the waste removal and the water tuning.

options.text: Two separate filters run side by side
options.explanation: It is one nephron doing both.
The bladder only stores what the kidneys have already decided.

options.text: Hormones from the adrenal gland do both jobs
options.explanation: ADH from the pituitary runs the water half; no hormone cleans the blood directly.

check.stem: State the two roles of the kidneys.
check.modelAnswer: Excreting toxic metabolic waste such as urea and substances in excess, and regulating the water content of the blood.

check.stem: Name the process by which the kidneys hold water levels steady.
Explain why excretion and osmoregulation are performed by the same organ.
check.modelAnswer: Both jobs need blood to be filtered: waste removal picks urea and surplus ions out of the bloodstream, and water tuning decides how much of the filtered water returns; a single filtering organ can do both in one pass, which is exactly what the nephron is built for.

check.stem: A heatwave leaves a person's blood both short of water and loaded with ions. Describe how the kidney responds.
check.modelAnswer: The kidney answers both problems at once: more water is reclaimed from the filtrate to defend blood volume, and the concentrated urine that results also carries out the surplus ions, so excretion and osmoregulation proceed together.

lessons.title: Osmoregulation and Cell Water
lessons.opening: Osmoregulation is homeostasis applied to water: keeping the osmotic balance of body fluids steady. Cells live or die by it, because water always moves across their membranes towards the more concentrated fluid. Two routes bring water in — drink and the water aerobic respiration makes — and two routes let it out uncontrolled, since every breath carries vapour away and sweat lifts more off the skin. The single adjustable outlet is urine, which is why the kidneys hold the whole balancing act together.
keyPoints: Osmoregulation keeps water and salt concentrations balanced across the body's membranes.
Cells gain water and swell in dilute surroundings; they lose water and shrivel in concentrated ones.
Too much water entering a cell can burst it; too little leaves it unable to work.
Water enters the body from the diet and as a product of respiration.
Water leaves via the lungs and skin without control, but urine volume is adjustable.

low.restatement: Cells need steady water: too much swells and bursts them, too little shrivels them.
low.analogy: A balloon left in the rain swells until it pops; one left in the sun shrinks — cells face the same two fates.
low.examPointer: Pair each extreme with its consequence — lysis for swelling, death for dehydration — in written answers.

medium.restatement: Water in from drink and respiration; out through breath, sweat and — controllably — urine.
medium.analogy: A household budget: some bills are fixed, but one expense is adjustable, and that one keeps the books balanced.
medium.examPointer: When asked how the body controls water, name urine as the adjustable route and the kidneys as the controller.

check.stem: What happens to cells surrounded by fluid that is too dilute?

options.text: Water moves in and they swell, possibly bursting
options.explanation: Dilute surroundings pull water into the cells.

options.text: Water moves out and they shrivel
options.explanation: That is the concentrated-surroundings outcome.

options.text: Nothing changes because membranes block water
options.explanation: Water crosses membranes freely by osmosis.
Swelling does not drive division.

check.stem: Which of these is a source of water for the body?

options.explanation: Respiration releases water as one of its products.

options.text: Water absorbed from the air by skin
options.explanation: Skin loses water; it does not harvest it from air.

options.text: Water pumped in by the heart
options.explanation: The heart moves blood, not new water.
The kidneys only move water between blood and urine.

check.stem: Which water loss route can the body actually control?

options.text: Urine volume, adjusted by the kidneys
options.explanation: Only the urinary output is adjustable.
Every breath carries water away regardless of need.
Sweating follows temperature, not water accounting.

options.text: None of them can be controlled
options.explanation: One route — urine — is precisely controlled.

check.stem: Why do cells stop working efficiently when they lose too much water?

options.text: Their chemistry needs water, and dehydration leaves too little for reactions
options.explanation: Cell reactions run in water; short of it, the machinery stalls.
Bursting is the too-much-water outcome.
Membranes persist; the contents are the problem.
The failure is chemical, not a nuclear switch-off.

check.stem: What carries ions and a small amount of urea out through the skin?

options.explanation: Sweat is the salty fluid that lifts ions and traces of urea away.
Breath carries vapour, not ions or urea.
Urine leaves via the urethra; sweat is a separate secretion.
Tears are one gland's output, not the skin's general route.

check.modelAnswer: Osmoregulation is the maintenance of steady water and salt concentrations in the body fluids.

check.stem: Name the two ways water enters the body.
check.modelAnswer: Water taken in with food and drink, and water produced by aerobic respiration.

check.stem: Explain why too much water in the blood can be as dangerous as too little.
check.modelAnswer: Excess blood water dilutes the fluids around cells, so osmosis drives water into them until they swell and may burst; too little water pulls water out so they dehydrate and their reactions stop — both extremes destroy the steady conditions cells require.

check.stem: A patient on a drip receives too much fluid too fast. Explain the risk to red blood cells.
check.modelAnswer: The extra fluid dilutes the plasma, so water flows by osmosis into the red blood cells; they swell beyond what the membrane tolerates and may burst, which is exactly the lysis risk that osmoregulation normally prevents.

glossary.definition: The keeping of water and salt concentrations in the body fluids steady across membranes.
The maintenance of constant internal conditions despite changes outside.
The bursting of a cell after too much water enters it by osmosis.
